extracted.intended_audience: law students, maritime lawyers, naval officers, merchants and masters concerned with prize, capture, and neutrality rules
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains legal principles governing prize courts, licences to trade, ransom/recapture/salvage, and the rights and duties of neutral nations and their subjects in wartime maritime commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appraisement and security on doubtful prize captures
rubrics_metrics.description: If on the preparatory examination there arises a doubt ... whether the capture is prize or not, the ship and cargo is appraised by persons named on the part of the captor, and is delivered up to the claimants, on their giving good and sufficient security to pay to the captor the full value, according to the appraisement, if the ship is adjudged lawful prize by the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimant entitled to immediate possession upon giving security; captor cannot obtain possession except on claimant's refusal. After sentence of condemnation captor has right to possession; execution of sentence is not suspended by an appeal, but the appellant must give security to restore cargo or value if sentence reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction of Prize Courts (where they can sit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prize Court of an Ally cannot condemn. Prize or no prize is a question belonging exclusively to the courts of the country of the captor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize Courts of the captor may sit in co-belligerent or ally country but not in neutral territory; courts of captor are responsible to inspect captors' conduct; cannot lawfully act in neutral territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality and consequences of Prize Court judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the Court of the capturing nation is conclusive upon the question of property in the captured thing. Its sentence settles all further dispute between claimants; and if that sentence is manifestly unjust, or against the Law of Nations, the state is alone responsible, and not the captors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unjust sentence is a ground for reprisals; numerous treaties permit reprisals only in case of 'denial of justice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of capture on immoveable property
rubrics_metrics.description: Immoveable possessions, lands, towns, provinces ... become the property of the enemy who makes himself master of them; but it is only by the treaty of peace, or the entire subjugation and extinction of the state to which those towns and provinces belonged, that the acquisition is completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties cannot safely purchase conquered land until sovereign renounces it by treaty or loses sovereignty; until confirmation it is liable to be divested by jus postliminii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passports and safe-conducts non-transferability and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Passports, and Safe-conducts ... insure safety to persons in passing and repassing, or to certain things during their conveyance. The person named in the Passport cannot transfer his privilege to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They promise security wherever the grantor has authority; interpreted by same rules of liberality and good faith as other sovereign acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licences as dispensation from laws of war
rubrics_metrics.description: A Licence granted by a state ... is a dispensation on its own side of the Laws of War, as far as its terms can be fairly construed. The adverse party may justly consider such licence as a ground of capture and confiscation per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize Courts of issuing state must consider them lawful relaxations; in the granting country licences are rigidly interpreted as exceptions to general rules, but not with pedantic accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of licences (good faith and unavoidable obstacles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court must confine itself to a reasonable explanation of the terms ... and cannot alter or dispense with conditions considered as essential by the Government granting the license. If the court extends by favourable interpretation, it does so only where there is a total absence of bad faith, and where unavoidable obstacles have been thrown in the way of exact compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is want of good faith or departure beyond necessity, the court will not mitigate penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted deviations in vessel nationality under a licence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an essential deviation from the licence, if ships of other countries than those designated in the license are employed; provided those other countries have the same political bearing towards this kingdom as those mentioned in the licence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But substituting a ship of a country at war for a neutral or native ship at will is not indifferent and may vitiate the licence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent misrepresentation of vessel nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an enemy's ship was represented to be neutral, and under that disguise obtained a licence and was navigated, the ship and freight were condemned; and the cargo would have been involved ... had it been shown that the owner of the cargo was privy to the fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of licence protection for cargo (enumeration of goods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The licence must be looked to for the enumeration of goods that are to be protected by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best endeavour should be made to follow the enumeration. Taking non-enumerated articles by mistake is not fatal, but essential and fraudulent departure is total defeasance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal restriction of licences (who may act under them)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a licence is granted to one person, it cannot be made to extend to the protection of all other persons who may be permitted by that person to take advantage of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licence names A and B 'as for themselves or their agents or the bearers of their bill of lading', only A and B as importers, their agents, or those holding bills of lading transferred to them are entitled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on merchants acting under import licences
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a licence to import, the British merchant must not also be the exporter. He is not permitted under such a licence to go to the enemy's country, and there act as an enemy's merchant, carrying on the export trade of that country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licence territory and voyage compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Voyage, also, the merchant must follow the licence. It is vitiated by changing the place of shipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviation from course cannot be tolerated except under irresistible necessity; touching at intermediate ports under a licence for direct voyage is a violation (presumption of change of destination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal limits and retrospective effect of licences
rubrics_metrics.description: When the period for which a licence has been granted has expired, it no longer has any operation. A licence cannot be antedated, and if granted subsequent to capture it is no protection against condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where due diligence prevented performance by accident, courts have sometimes protected expired licences if prevention was excusable; licences are prospective, not retroactive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ransom contracts validity and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Ransom contracts are valid when municipal regulations do not intervene; the captain of the captor engages for release in consideration of a sum, and the master delivers a hostage as security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ransom generally cannot exceed the value of the ship; captor bound to take vessel or its value if abandoned; captor must maintain the hostage (item in ransom bill); remedy to enforce ransom during war may be in captor's courts or via action by hostage in his own country's courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture restitution principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the recapture ought to be restored depends on whether the captor has become full proprietor of the prize, to the total extinction of the rights of the first proprietor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under laws of war the right and power of possession is in the captor; right of property remains in the proprietor until peace. Generally recaptured property ought to be restored to original owner on just repayment of costs and damages (salvage), unless recapture illegality precludes indemnification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvage as indemnity for recaptors
rubrics_metrics.description: The costs and damages paid to the recaptor are termed Salvage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient rules varied; modern English practice leans to restitution upon salvage for merchant property; but no salvage if property was not in possession or so nearly under grasp of the enemy as to be rescued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — recaptured ships converted into ships of war
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recaptured ship ... shall appear to have been by them 'set forth as a ship or vessel of war,' the said ship or vessel shall not be restored to the former owners ... but shall be adjudged lawful prize for the benefit of the captors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion into national force extinguishes former owner's title; 'setting forth' need not be sailing with a commission—use as part of national force by competent authority suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material test for recapture — effectual possession
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of recapture, the material question is whether the enemy have an effectual possession; not necessarily complete possession by condemnation, but possession that, if not interrupted, would have enabled the captor to exercise rights of war over her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession need not be long; examples show various degrees (e.g., enemy aboarding, bringing under control, or compelling to port) that constitute effectual possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration of allied or neutral recaptured property
rubrics_metrics.description: England restores the Recaptured Property of her Allies, on the payment of salvage; but if instances can be given of British property retaken by them, and condemned as prize, the Court of Admiralty will determine their cases according to their own rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern nations generally do not grant salvage on recapture of neutral vessels, on the principle that liberation of a neutral would be ordered by tribunals of the captor's country; exceptions have occurred in extraordinary hostile practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jus postliminii — restoration on re-acquisition of sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Things taken by the enemy are restored to their former owner, upon coming again under the power of the nation to which they formerly belonged; termed jus postliminii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies more readily to real property than moveables; during war right of postliminy can only be claimed in belligerent tribunals, not neutral courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for invalid seizures (due diligence standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the capture is not justifiable, a captor is answerable for every damage. But if a seizure is justifiable, all that the law requires is that the captor shall be held responsible for due diligence; it is not enough that the captor should use as much caution as he would in his own affairs, the law requires that there should be no deficiency of due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize-master's refusal to take a pilot resulting in loss led to restitution; when property is entrusted to another, owner's care may be criterion, but capture is compulsory and removes owner responsibility for prize-master's imprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and duties of neutral nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutral Nations are those who, in time of war, take no part in the contest, but remain common friends to both parties, without favouring the arms of the one to the prejudice of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutrality consists in (1) giving no assistance when no obligation to give it; nor voluntarily furnishing troops, arms, ammunition, or anything of direct use in war; (2) in whatever does not relate to war, a neutral must not refuse to one party what she grants to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified neutrality by treaty
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutrality rules do not apply to engagements by treaty, to which the Neutral may be bound previous to war; e.g., engagement to furnish limited succour or to open ports to armed vessels of an ally with prizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutrality may be qualified to admit vessels of war with prizes of one belligerent and exclude the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of neutral territory and limits of belligerent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rights of War can be exercised only within the territory of the belligerent powers, upon the high seas, or in a territory belonging to no one. To make use of neutral territory for the proximate purposes of war cannot be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remote uses such as procuring provisions are tolerated; neutral territory presumed to extend three English miles from shore; neutral territory sanctity is high and must be proved by clear evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of belligerent property within neutral territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The general inviolability of neutral character ... protects the property of belligerents within the neutral territory. If the enemy be attacked, or any capture made under neutral protection, the neutral is bound to redress the injury, and effect restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: captures in neutral bays were restored upon complaint to neutral government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on belligerent warships using neutral harbours as stations
rubrics_metrics.description: An armed ship has no right to lie in a neutral harbour, in order to make it an habitual station for her captures, as that would be a continuous direct infringement on neutral trade with the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accidentally in neutral port and an enemy comes, ship may go out and fight beyond neutral ground; captors should not station at mouth of neutral rivers to exercise rights of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chased vessels entering neutral ports and the neutrality response
rubrics_metrics.description: Bynkershoek maintained vessels may be chased into neutral territory and there captured, but the true rule is that voluntary entrance into neutral territory with hostile purposes is unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration takes place only on application of the neutral government whose territory was violated; the neutral's protection grounds invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent of neutral state for bringing prizes into neutral ports
rubrics_metrics.description: Though a belligerent vessel may not enter within neutral jurisdiction for hostile purposes, she may, consistently with a state of neutrality (unless prohibited by the neutral power), bring her prize into the neutral port and sell it there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent of neutral state is necessary; neutral may permit certain acts by treaty or regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom and risks of neutral commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: A neutral has a right to pursue his accustomed commerce, and he may become the carrier of the enemy's goods, without being subject to confiscation of the ship, or of the neutral articles on board; though not without the risk of having the voyage interrupted by the seizure of the hostile property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If enemy effects on board a neutral ship are seized, captor must pay freight to master; neutrals voluntarily expose themselves to risk by placing goods on hostile ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of neutral effects found on enemy ships
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of neutrals found in an enemy's ship, are to be restored to the owners, against whom there is no right of confiscation, but without allowance for detainder, decay, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutrals voluntarily expose themselves to these accidents when embarking goods in a hostile ship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captor's entitlement to freight upon seizure
rubrics_metrics.description: When an enemy's ship, containing free goods, is taken, if the captor carries the goods to the port of destination, he is entitled to the freight. He stands in the place of the owner of the ship, and performs the specific contract between the owner and charterer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If captor does not perform the original voyage, freight may not be allowed; freight may be allowed if goods are carried to the captor's country or appropriate ports; captor remains answerable for misconduct or injury (set-off).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty conventions may alter capture rules (free ships/free goods)
rubrics_metrics.description: This Rule is often Changed by Convention; and it is generally stipulated that 'free ships shall make free goods.' The converse ... does not of necessity hold, 'enemy's ships do not make enemy's goods.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules as to neutral/enemy goods vary by treaty; national practice differs and treaties can supersede general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral goods on armed belligerent vessels (national differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America, Neutral Goods laden on an Armed Belligerent Vessel are still protected, but in England it is different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Wm. Scott: if neutral puts goods on board a ship of force which will be defended by force, he betrays intention to resist visitation and search and withdraws from protection of neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale and purchase of enemy vessels by neutrals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Purchase of Ships from the enemy is a liberty that has not been denied to neutral merchants (though by France it may be forbidden).
